meta.title: Evaluation metrics for creativity ratings: Cronbach's alpha, Krippendorff's alpha, Spearman-Brown, JRT reliability
meta.purpose: Reference for verifying that a manuscript describes these metrics, their limitations, and their appropriate use in a fully crossed block versus a sparse rating design correctly.
meta.provenance: Standard psychometric results stated from general knowledge; no numbers here were computed on the manuscript's data. Companion file: jrt_reference.json (JRT model, estimation, scoring).

definitions.fully_crossed_block: Every judge rates every product in the block (complete product x judge matrix).
definitions.sparse_design: Each product is rated by only a subset of the judges; subsets differ between products.
definitions.key_distinction: Reliability of an aggregated score (how well a mean or model score separates products) is a different quantity from agreement of individual ratings (whether judges assign the same value). Do not use the two terms interchangeably.

cronbach_alpha.measures: Reliability (internal consistency) of the sum or mean rating across k judges: the share of variance in the composite that is consistent across judges.
cronbach_alpha.formula: alpha = k/(k-1) * (1 - sum of judge variances / variance of the sum score). Equivalent to a two-way consistency intraclass correlation for the mean of k judges.
cronbach_alpha.level: The composite of k judges. Increases with the number of judges.
properties: Based on covariances between judges; additive severity differences between judges do not lower it.
It is not an index of agreement. Describing it as 'inter-rater agreement' is imprecise; 'inter-rater reliability of the mean rating' or 'consistency' is correct.
limitations: Requires a complete product x judge matrix.
Assumes judges are essentially tau-equivalent (equally good indicators) with uncorrelated errors; with unequal judges it is a lower bound to the reliability of the mean.
One error variance for all products; gives no product-specific precision.
Refers to the unweighted mean; says nothing about differences in judge discrimination or scale use.
Depends on the variance of the products in the sample (restricted range lowers it).

in_sparse_design.status: Not appropriate as the reliability of the available scores.
why_it_overstates: Listwise deletion: only products rated by all judges are kept. Ratings are dropped, the remaining subset may be small or unrepresentative, and the coefficient describes a full-panel mean that most products never received.

Pairwise covariances: the coefficient is assembled for a complete panel of k judges, i.e. it assumes a design that does not exist. Each real product is rated by fewer judges, so its mean is less reliable than the coefficient implies.
In both cases the result overestimates the reliability of the scores actually obtained in the sparse design.
It additionally ignores that means from different judge subsets are confounded with judge severity, which adds error that alpha does not count.
in_sparse_design.wording_note: Correct claim: Cronbach's alpha overstates the reliability (consistency) of sparse-design scores because it either discards ratings or presumes a fully crossed design. Avoid saying it overstates 'agreement' without qualification, since alpha is not an agreement coefficient; if the manuscript uses 'agreement' loosely, flag it.

krippendorff_alpha.measures: Chance-corrected agreement of individual ratings: whether judges assign the same value to the same product.
krippendorff_alpha.formula: alpha = 1 - D_o / D_e, where D_o is the observed disagreement among ratings of the same product and D_e the disagreement expected if ratings were assigned to products at random. The difference function depends on the chosen measurement level (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio).
krippendorff_alpha.level: A single rating. Does not increase systematically with the number of judges.
properties: Handles any number of judges and missing ratings natively, so it is computable in sparse designs.
Systematic severity differences between judges count as disagreement (absolute agreement).
With the interval metric it is close to a one-way single-rating intraclass correlation.
Usually much lower than Cronbach's alpha on the same data, because it refers to single ratings and penalises severity differences.
limitations: Not the reliability of an aggregated score; a low value does not imply that the mean rating or a model-based score is unreliable.
Penalises exactly the judge tendencies (severity, scale use) that JRT models and accounts for.
Value depends on the chosen measurement level; this must be reported (ordinal is the natural choice for 1-5 ratings).
Sensitive to the spread of products: low variance between products lowers it.
One coefficient for the whole panel; no judge-specific or product-specific information.

spearman_brown.measures: Not a coefficient of its own but a projection: the reliability of the mean of k ratings, given the reliability of a single rating.
spearman_brown.formula: rel_k = k * r_1 / (1 + (k - 1) * r_1), where r_1 is the single-rating reliability (e.g. a single-rating intraclass correlation from a variance-components model).
spearman_brown.relations: Standardised Cronbach's alpha equals Spearman-Brown applied to the mean inter-judge correlation.
spearman_brown.use: Classical estimate of the reliability of raw mean ratings when products have fewer than all judges: step a single-rating reliability up to the number of ratings a product actually has.
limitations: Assumes parallel, interchangeable judges with equal error variance; ignores differences in discrimination and scale use.

The result depends on which single-rating reliability is used. When different products are rated by different judges, judge severity variance is part of the error, so an absolute-agreement / one-way single-rating coefficient is the appropriate input; a consistency coefficient would overstate.
With varying numbers of ratings per product there is no single k; use the actual k per product or state the summary used (e.g. harmonic mean).
Gives one reliability per k, not a product-specific standard error.

jrt_reliability.measures: Reliability of the model-based product scores (EAP) from the fitted judge response model, built from product-specific standard errors.

variants.empirical: Var(EAP) / (Var(EAP) + mean of squared posterior SDs). Describes the scores actually obtained; valid with missing ratings because each product contributes its own standard error.
variants.expected_marginal: Average over a N(0,1) product distribution of I(theta) / (I(theta) + 1), where I is the summed information of a stated set of judges. Assumes every product is rated by all judges in that set.
variants.conditional: I(theta) / (I(theta) + 1) at a given theta; shows where on the scale precision is high or low.

properties: Accounts for judge differences in severity, scale use and discrimination.
Precision can differ between products and along the scale.
Places products rated by different judge subsets on one scale, provided the design is connected.
limitations: Model-dependent: takes the fitted model at face value. Overestimated discriminations or violated local independence inflate it.
Standard errors of scores condition on the estimated judge parameters and omit their uncertainty.
Relies on the N(0,1) latent distribution (identification, EAP shrinkage).
Requires a connected design and enough ratings per judge and category for stable parameters.
Expected reliability computed over all judges overstates precision in a sparse design; the empirical version is the one that reflects the real design.
Refers to a different score than Cronbach's alpha (weighted model score versus unweighted mean), so a higher value is not by itself evidence of more accurate scores.

fully_crossed_block.reliability_of_mean_rating: Cronbach's alpha (standard in the consensual assessment literature); interpret as a lower bound when judges are unequal.
fully_crossed_block.reliability_of_model_scores: JRT empirical reliability; expected and conditional reliability are also meaningful here because the full panel rated every product.
fully_crossed_block.agreement_description: Krippendorff's alpha (ordinal) as a supplementary description of how interchangeable judges are; not the reliability of the aggregate.
fully_crossed_block.spearman_brown: Not needed for the full panel; useful only to project reliability for fewer or more judges.

sparse_design.reliability_of_model_scores: JRT empirical reliability is the appropriate primary index.
sparse_design.classical_counterpart_for_raw_means: Single-rating intraclass correlation (absolute agreement, from a variance-components model) stepped up with Spearman-Brown to the typical or actual number of ratings per product.
sparse_design.agreement_description: Krippendorff's alpha (ordinal), computable with missing data; descriptive only.
sparse_design.not_appropriate: Cronbach's alpha as the reliability of the sparse-design scores: it overstates, because it either drops ratings (listwise) or assumes a fully crossed design that is not the real one (pairwise). JRT expected reliability over the whole judge pool has the same problem unless explicitly presented as a hypothetical full-panel value.

statements_to_flag_in_a_manuscript: Cronbach's alpha described as agreement between judges.
Cronbach's alpha reported for a sparse design without stating how missing ratings were handled and that it refers to a complete panel.
Krippendorff's alpha reported without its measurement level, or interpreted as the reliability of mean or model-based scores.
Direct comparison of Cronbach's and Krippendorff's alpha as if they were on the same level (composite versus single rating).
Spearman-Brown applied without stating the single-rating coefficient and the k used.
JRT expected (marginal) reliability presented as the reliability of sparse-design scores.
A higher JRT reliability than Cronbach's alpha presented as proof that JRT scores are more accurate.
